en: The Gautamī Śikṣā belonging to the Sāmaveda: Now, there are thirty-three consonants.
The *sparśas*, the *antasthas*, and the *ūṣmans*:

therein, the *sparśas* are twenty-five, beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*; the four *antasthas* are *ya, ra, la, va*; and the four *ūṣmans* are *ha, śa, ṣa, sa*. Where multiple consonants are joined one above the other, that is termed a *saṃyoga* (conjunction). Thus, the preceding vowel-less syllable [is formed]. Now, the *saṃyoga-piṇḍa* (consonantal cluster) is of three kinds: the iron-cluster (*ayasa-piṇḍa*), the wood-cluster (*dāru-piṇḍa*), and likewise the wool-cluster (*ūrṇā-piṇḍa*).
A *piṇḍa* consisting of *yama* (consonants) together with *antaḥsthas* (semivowels) is a "wooden" (*dāru*) *piṇḍa*.

A *piṇḍa* devoid of *yamas* and *antaḥsthas* is a "woolen" (*ūrṇā*) *piṇḍa*. Thus, when there is a combination of *antaḥsthas* and *yamas*, no distinction is perceived; one should know that such a *yama* is bodiless (*aśarīra*), for the *antaḥstha* is the leader of the *piṇḍas*.
Now, there are twenty *anantyās* (finals), which are: *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa*; *kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha*; *ga, ja, ḍa, da, ba*.

Now, *gha*, *jha*, *ḍha*, *dha*, and *bha* are the five final [consonants], namely *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*. Then, the four non-final [consonants] are *sa*, *ya*, *ma*, and *ra*. In the combination of a non-final and a final consonant—where the non-final precedes and the non-final follows, and there is no intervening [vowel]—the *yamas* (nasalized counterparts) reside there without doubt.
Now, all consonants undergo doubling, with the exception of twelve syllables; these are *kha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *tha*, and *pha*.

Some authorities maintain that the *gha*, *jha*, *ḍha*, *dha*, and *bha* [substitute consonants] occur after the letter *ra*; furthermore, if they occur between *ra* and *ha*, then in all cases, a consonant following a vowel— excluding *ra* and *ha*— is elided.

One transcends beyond those two, yet one does not transcend what follows the *upadhmānīya*, the *anusvāra*, and the *jihvāmūlīya*, as well as that which follows a *visarjanīya*. Regarding the suffix *tsap*: *kṣaḥ tsapratyaye*, *kṣaḥ tsapratyaye*.
Now, here are examples of words consisting of two syllables: two *takāra*s [occur] in the phrase "tasmātte sattamāḥ," just as in "priyavetteva bhavati."
There are two *na*s when they say "namasyanti" and "śanno devīr unnayāmi"; there are two *ja*s when [it says] "yaj jāyathāḥ" and "ujjihānā asthimajjā";
there are two *ma*s when [it says] "yam mitram tan manye" and "śam maghavan."
The two *ca*-sounds are those [occurring] in "yadadyakacca" and "paramāccid";
the two *sa*-sounds are those in "jātamandhaso" and "punānasso'gniḥ samidhā";
the two *ya*-sounds are those in "dhānañjayyaḥ" and "nivarttasva". These are the *bhārgava* sāmans, which are to be chanted quickly.

There are two *dakāra*s: in *yad dūre* and *yad didhṛkṣe*. Maudgalya Āruṇi [says] there are two *lakāra*s: one should draw upward from the heavenly world with the arms; this is indeed by means of these worlds. There are two *ṅakāra*s: in *ṛśyavrata* and *ṛśyāsa indrabhuṅ ṅiti maghavan indra bhuṅ ṅiti prabhuṅ ṅiti*; Indra is purified by the *tasa* [suffixes]. Thus and so forth. 4.2345.
The letters *ca* and *cha* signify "he went to Indra";
the letters *ta* and *tha* signify "you know";
the letters *da* and *dha* signify "pure."
The syllables *baka* and *bhaka* are "eating water" (*abbhakṣa*); the third is *yaṇve*;
*repha* and *ṣakāra* are "the most excellent in rain and soma" (*arṣāsomadyumattama*); *edaṃ barhiḥ* is "the *ra* and *ha* separated" (*vihruta*); and *harau*.
He has shown his power in the sun;
he has touched the waters in the sky.
Having stepped upon heaven, he has made the earth tremble; he has caused the ocean to roar. He has struck down the demon Pipru.
The *iḍā* [sāman] (2345) and so forth— these five, as well as others such as the *sarpa-sāman*, *dharma-rocanā*, and *abhīvarta* mentioned in the *Karaṇa* [section].

Restraining, exerting, striving, and concentrating—may the worlds of light shine for you. O subduer of immortality, or indeed by those strengths, the first [consonant] is nasalized when followed by another [consonant] produced in the same place and organ; this is the prohibition of *krama*. This is the prohibition of *krama*.
Now, here are examples of three-syllable words: *akṣaram*, *kakapāḥ*, *tamṛbhasambhavāḥ*, *yacchikṣasi*, *cacachāḥ*, *tvāmiddhi*, *dadadhāḥ*, *traiśoke*, *śaśavā*, *viśvohāi*.
The Brahmins say "Brahmā," the Vaiṣṇavas say "Viṣṇu," and the Pārṣṇikas say "Pṛśni."
"O you who have swift-moving chariots," thus they say, desiring all things;
"may we obtain all desires. Such are the seven [verses] beginning with these, [recited] at the *āmr̥ta* [offering].
O descendant of Raghu, place your long foot in the middle [of my head],
and bend down near the edge of your foot.
In *gauśṛṅga*, there is then *tatasāstaraṇi*; in *itsaṣāsatī*, there are six *ṭaṭasāḥ*;
and in *khaḍge*, there are *ḍaḍagāḥ*.

"O hunchbacked one, the thunderbolt-born [Vajra] has shattered the aged ones; Varuṇa, the moon, and the Sāman-singers have caused the ocean to swell, shining forth widely"—such are the eight [verses], beginning with this. 2345. 8.
The syllable *ka-kha* indicates *rākṣasī*; *ṅa-ṅa-kha* indicates *mūrkha*; and *śa-ṅ-ṅa-kha* indicates *śaṅkha*.
The wise one, having understood what is beneficial in that manner, manifests it as it truly is; he who is worthy of honor,
having conquered through effort,
makes firm that which was difficult to establish.

"tubbhyaṃ babhayāḥ saṃṣaḍahaḥ," "iti nanaṣāḥ rakakāḥ," "arkkapuṣpe sāmnī," "arkko devānāṃ parame viyo viyo mā 2345," "na rkasya devāḥ parame viyo viyo mā 2345"— these and others such as these are examples of [verses] consisting of three syllables, as has been stated, as has been stated.
Thus ends the first chapter.
Now, an illustration of four-syllable [words]: *sayamāyamābhyām*. First, regarding *sayamān*, as in *yathāgniḥ*, there are two *ga*-sounds and two *ya*-sounds.

In *yajjñau*, there are two *ja*s and two *ma*s; in *yunajmita*, there are two *ja*s and two *ma*s; in *vidmāhitvā*, there are two *da*s and two *ma*s; in *samante dadhāyama*, there are two *ma*s; in *bharāmeddhmaṃ kṛṇavāmā havīṃṣi tāyi gṛbbhṇīta*, there are *ba*, *bha*, *ya*, *ma*, *ṇa*, and *ka*.
"Unmṛdnītān" consists of the syllables *da*, *da*, *ya*, and *ma*;
"sagiḍḍhma" consists of the syllables *ḍa*, *ḍa*, *ya*, and *ma*; "pāppma" consists of the syllables *pa*, *pa*, *ya*, and *ma*.
The *vilamba* [melodies] are those beginning with "sauparṇe," "tatayamana-kārāḥ," "pratnām anu dyutaṃ," "ī ye iyāhāḥ," and so forth.
Now, for those excluding the *yama*, there are the *ṅaṅanayāḥ* beginning with "yathodan nyañca" and the *raṣaṣamāḥ* beginning with "kārṣmān vājī."
"O Indra, that which is trembling, that which is firm," thus [he says]; "the moon moves within the waters," thus [he says];

"the sinners in the Hārāyaṇa," thus [he says]; "the singers among the Śagdhyaus," thus [he says]; "O Lord of Might, the entire [world]," thus [he says]; "the Paṅkti [meter]," thus [he says]; "the fivefold [set]," thus [he says].
"Sthirasnu" and so forth are for the *pāpasvan* [chanters];
"prāṅṅkṣuḥ" and so forth are for the *naṅaka*s; "kaṇvarathantare," "rajañjayā," and "mārjyamānassuhastiya"—these and others [are used].
"Then they mount the swings," thus [the syllables] *ra-ha-ha-yāḥ*; "so indeed is the vow," thus *ba-ba-va-raḥ*;
"universal sovereigns, lords, with dogs," thus *śa-śa-ra-vāḥ*;
"fish, look! thus *ta-ta-sa-yāḥ*.

In the *śrautakakṣa*, there are *nanadarāḥ*; for Indra in the *madavana*, the pressed [soma] was offered; "for Indra, the one who is not to be harmed" (*ayajjvyaghaṭata*)—thus it is *jajavayāḥ*; "kaṇṭhya" means *ṇaṇaṭhayā*; "the final of the class" (*vargāntya*) means *nanatayāḥ*.
"Sunikkṣīti kakatasāḥ," "raśaśayāḥ prāpnuvat," "darśyāyato," and so forth; these are examples of [words] with five syllables. Now, here are examples of those with five syllables.
Just as in the case of "jyotir-gaur-āyuḥ" [the compound] is for three days; "sasatarāyāḥ" [is used] for sharpening;
"ṅaṅakaṣaṇāḥ" [is used] for that which is independent; and "nanatasavāḥ" [is used] in that context.
"viśvappsnyā" (VS 2.17) refers to the *papasanaya* [fingers];
"yuṅṅkṣvāhi" (VS 2.18) refers to the *ṅaṅakaṣavaḥ*;
"pārṣṇyoḥ" (VS 2.19) refers to the *raṣaṣaṇayaḥ*.
In *śaggdhvyāṃroha* there is *gagadhavayāḥ*; in *pūrṇāññjvyotyāviti* there is *ñañajavayāḥ*;
and in *huvejasikrayaṇṇṭsvatām* there is *ṇaṇaṭasavāḥ*.
The *tārkṣyasāman* verses are: *ra ka ka ṣa yāḥ*, *tārkṣyam ihā 1343 huvā 1 5 yimā 1656*, and so forth. Then the *sayamanas*:
with the verse beginning *atha sabuddhnyā*, one [recites] *dadhyam anayāḥ*;
with the verse beginning *duḥṣvapnyam sviti*, one [recites] *papayam anayāḥ*.
By the Queen of Serpents, O Jajaya-maṇaya; by the Mother of the Māṭṭṇya, O Ṭaṭaya-maṇaya;
for purification, O Gaghaya-maṇaya; the lord of you who are inviolable cows, O Dhenus, may he be established in nourishment. 23. U vā.
Those ending in *k* and *th* are those with *y* as the penultimate letter; those ending in *n* and *m* are those with *s* as the penultimate letter;
and those beginning with *g*, *dh*, *bh*, *kh*, *p*, or *ś* are those with *m* as the penultimate letter.
"From the head he breathed forth"—thus [the syllables] *ra*, *da*, *dha*, *ya*, *ma*, *na*, *kā*, *rāḥ*;
"from Kāverī arose the conqueror"—thus [the syllables] *ka*, *ā*, *ve*, *ra*, *ja*, *ja*, *ya*, *ma*, *kā*, *rāḥ*;
"through lack of understanding the fire rose from the earth"—thus *i*, *tya*, *bo*, *dha*, *adhi*, *agniḥ*, *jmaḥ*, *ud*, *ā*, *yi*, *ti*, *sūḥ*, *ā*; and so forth. 5.13.2.13.1–5.13.2.13.5.

Now, an illustration of the six syllables: in the *Aṅga* [section], beginning with *cakṣuṣyādau*, there are two *ka*s; *yamamaka-vakāra-yakāra* refers to the complete set of rules (*satrakārtsnya*); *ratatasanayāḥ*; and *apsādhyargghmavāham* consists of *ra-ga-ra-dha-ya-ma-ma-kāra*s. 6.
Now, one [example] of seven syllables has been cited in the *Maṅke Prātiśākhya*: "na hi na dhuñughuñkṣuṅṅkṣkṣvāvi," where there are the sounds ṅ, ṅ, ka, ṣ, ka, ṣ, and va.

Gautama stated: "There is no conjunct (saṃyoga) following a seven-syllable [word]; this is the 'Chain of Conjuncts' (*saṃyoga-śṛṅkhalā*), consisting of a thousand paths and adorned with various turns, according to the rules of the Sāmaveda. (7)
Thus ends the second chapter;
thus ends the Gautamī Śikṣā belonging to the Sāmaveda.
